commentary.bottom_line: Five small studies, most of them qualitative or simulated and none with a comparison group, suggest that engaging clinicians and patients early may yield tools that users rate as usable and interpretable. No study measured whether early engagement changes adoption, trust, or patient outcomes after deployment.

perspectives.view: All five studies report findings that favor the practice, but four are level 4 and one is a level 3 interview study with 12 stakeholders. None randomized or compared engaged versus non-engaged development, and four took place offline or in simulation. Risk of bias, indirectness, and imprecision lower certainty to very low.

An interface built from anesthesiology clinicians' stated needs received a mean System Usability Scale score of 82.5 from 25 clinicians. Interviewees in a real deployment described longitudinal, multidisciplinary engagement as a factor that helped algorithm performance carry into care. Neither study compared this approach with conventional design, so the added value of engagement remains unmeasured.

In a pre-post test on 4,235 pelvic films, hip fracture detection specificity rose from 0.84 to 0.93 after design thinking with clinicians, while sensitivity stayed at 0.97. Fewer false positives may reduce unnecessary workups, but the confidence intervals overlap, the test was offline, and no patient harm outcomes were recorded.

In community engagement studios, 21 patients judged the model's variables interpretable, suggested additional predictors, and said they wanted to discuss results with their providers. This finding suggests that patient input can surface expectations of human contact that developers might otherwise miss. No study reported whether that input changed the final design.

Providers in the same engagement study cited limited bandwidth as a barrier to discussing model results with patients, which points to a staffing cost that engagement can reveal but not resolve. No study reported the time, staff hours, or budget that early engagement required. The multi-society radiology statement recommends engaging clinicians before substantial development investment, but offers no cost data.

No test reported the insurance status, language, literacy, or care setting of participants, so the evidence cannot show whether engagement captured the needs of disadvantaged groups. The HEAAL framework describes procedures for identifying disadvantaged subgroups, but no supplied study evaluated those procedures.

commentary.research_gap: No study compared tools developed with early stakeholder engagement against tools developed without it, and none followed a deployed tool to measure adoption, sustained use, trust, or patient outcomes. Studies are needed that describe which stakeholders were engaged, how their input changed the design, what the engagement cost, and whether downstream results differed.
commentary.underserved_note: None of the five tests reported whether participants included Medicaid enrollees, safety-net patients or clinicians, people with limited English proficiency, or people with low literacy; one study engaged 21 patients through community studios without describing their characteristics. Health systems serving these populations therefore cannot assume that engagement methods tested so far reflect their patients' needs or trust concerns.
